title: Maternal Omega-3 Fatty Acid Exposure During Pregnancy and Childhood Allergic Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis
content: Background: Prenatal exposure to omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFAs) may influence immune development, but associations with allergic disorders in childhood remain inconsistent. Objective: To evaluate the association of maternal omega-3 exposure during pregnancy with childhood asthma, wheeze, eczema, and allergic nasal disease. Methods: This systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis included 13 independent study populations contributing 22 outcome-specific estimates. Prenatal dietary intake, biomarkers, fish consumption, and supplementation were considered. Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation with modified Knapp-Hartung inference; pooled effects are presented as log odds ratios (logORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).Results: For asthma (k = 5), pooled logOR was -0.240 (95% CI -0.444 to -0.036; p = 0.031; I² = 0.0%). For wheeze (k = 5), logOR was -0.071 (95% CI -0.176 to 0.035; p = 0.137; I² = 31.3%). For eczema (k = 7), logOR was -0.106 (95% CI -0.839 to 0.627; p = 0.736; I² = 78.4%). For allergic nasal disease (k = 5), logOR was -0.078 (95% CI -0.461 to 0.305; p = 0.602; I² = 72.8%). Conclusions: Higher maternal omega-3 exposure was associated with lower pooled odds of childhood asthma, whereas associations for the other outcomes were statistically inconclusive. Differences in exposure definitions, study designs, and allergy phenotypes limit causal interpretation.
